title: Oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function in early Parkinson's disease: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
abstract: Trehalose, a naturally occurring disaccharide with autophagy-enhancing properties, has shown neuroprotective effects in preclinical models of Parkinson's disease, but clinical evidence in patients has been lacking.
We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 48 patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease to test whether oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function.

Patients received oral trehalose 5 g twice daily or matching placebo for 6 months, with the change in the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale part III (UPDRS-III) motor score as the primary endpoint.

At 6 months, the trehalose group improved by a mean of 6.2 points on the UPDRS-III motor score, compared with a mean improvement of 1.1 points in the placebo group (difference 5.1 points, 95% CI 2.4 to 7.8, p = 0.008).
Timed finger tapping and gait speed improved concordantly, and the benefit was not explained by changes in levodopa dose.
Serum alpha-synuclein oligomer concentrations decreased by 21% in the trehalose group and were unchanged in the placebo group.
Oral trehalose supplementation was well tolerated, with mild transient diarrhoea the most frequent adverse event.
These findings indicate that oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function in patients with early Parkinson's disease and support its further evaluation as a disease-modifying therapy.

title: Oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function in patients with early Parkinson's disease: an independent 12-month replication.
abstract: A previous 6-month randomized trial reported that oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function in early Parkinson's disease; we sought to replicate that finding over a longer treatment horizon.
In an independent open-label study, 36 patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease received oral trehalose 5 g twice daily for 12 months.
The primary outcome was the change in the UPDRS-III motor score, assessed by a rater blinded to treatment allocation.
Over 12 months, patients improved by a mean of 7.4 points on the UPDRS-III motor score, with the largest gains in timed finger tapping and gait speed.
The improvement in motor function correlated with the decrease in serum alpha-synuclein oligomer concentration.
Adverse events were limited to mild transient diarrhoea, and no patient withdrew because of side effects.
Our results confirm that oral trehalose supplementation improves motor function in patients with early Parkinson's disease and suggest that the benefit persists at 12 months.

title: Oral trehalose does not improve motor function in Parkinson's disease: a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial.
abstract: Preclinical data and small open-label studies in early-stage cohorts suggested that oral trehalose supplementation might improve motor function in Parkinson's disease, but adequately powered clinical evidence has been missing.
We conducted a 12-month, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 212 patients with moderate-stage Parkinson's disease.
Patients received oral trehalose 10 g daily or matching placebo, with the change in the UPDRS-III motor score as the primary endpoint.
At 12 months, the mean change in the UPDRS-III motor score was 0.9 points in the trehalose group and 1.0 points in the placebo group (difference 0.1 points, 95% CI -1.4 to 1.6, p = 0.89).
Secondary motor outcomes, including timed finger tapping, gait speed, and freezing-of-gait episodes, likewise showed no difference between the treatment groups.
Serum alpha-synuclein oligomer concentrations did not change in either group.
Trehalose was well tolerated, and adverse events did not differ from placebo.

In patients with established Parkinson's disease, oral trehalose supplementation did not improve motor function relative to placebo, and the positive findings reported in small early-stage cohorts were not reproduced.

title: Trehalose induces autophagy and clears aggregated alpha-synuclein in cultured neuronal cells.
abstract: Aggregated alpha-synuclein is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease, and enhancing its clearance is a candidate therapeutic strategy.
We examined the effect of trehalose, a disaccharide reported to act as an autophagy inducer, on alpha-synuclein accumulation in cultured neuronal cell lines.
In SH-SY5Y cells stably overexpressing alpha-synuclein, trehalose increased the number of autophagic vacuoles and LC3-II levels, indicating enhanced macroautophagy.
Trehalose lowered intracellular aggregated alpha-synuclein by approximately 40% over 72 hours, an effect abolished by the autophagy inhibitor bafilomycin A1.
The induction of autophagy by trehalose was independent of mTOR signalling, distinguishing it from rapamycin-like mechanisms.
These mechanistic results are confined to in vitro neuronal cultures and do not address whether trehalose affects patients or any clinical outcome in vivo.

title: Trehalose preserves protein structure during freeze-drying and long-term storage of biopharmaceuticals.
abstract: Trehalose is widely used as a stabilizing excipient in lyophilized protein formulations, but the structural basis of its protective effect remains incompletely characterised.
We compared trehalose, sucrose, and sorbitol as cryo- and lyoprotectants for two model enzymes during freeze-drying and 12 months of storage at elevated temperature.

Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and differential scanning calorimetry showed that trehalose maintained the native secondary structure of both proteins to a greater degree than the alternative excipients.
Residual activity after storage was 96% for the trehalose formulation versus 78% and 71% for sucrose and sorbitol, respectively.
The glass transition temperature of the trehalose matrix exceeded that of the other sugars, consistent with its superior stabilization.
Trehalose is an effective stabilizer of dried protein pharmaceuticals, a formulation property unrelated to any biological activity in living cells.

title: Supervised exercise improves motor function and gait in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Pharmacological treatment of Parkinson's disease incompletely relieves motor signs, and interest in non-pharmacological interventions has grown.
We systematically reviewed randomized controlled trials of supervised exercise programmes in patients with Parkinson's disease, pooling 34 trials enrolling 1,588 patients.
Supervised exercise was associated with a standardized mean improvement of 0.46 in UPDRS-III motor score relative to no-intervention controls.
Gait speed, balance, and freezing-of-gait severity improved concordantly, with the largest effects for treadmill training and resistance exercise.
Benefits were maintained for up to 6 months after the end of the programme but declined thereafter.
Supervised exercise is an effective adjunct for improving motor function in Parkinson's disease, and its optimal intensity and duration remain to be determined.

title: Vitamin D deficiency increases all-cause mortality risk in a large United States population cohort.
abstract: Vitamin D has been proposed to influence the risk of death from cardiovascular causes, cancer, and other chronic conditions, but population-level evidence on its association with all-cause mortality has been inconsistent.
We examined the association between serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration and all-cause mortality in a prospective cohort of 9,435 community-dwelling adults enrolled in a national health survey.
Vitamin D deficiency was defined as a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration below 30 nmol/L, and participants were followed for a median of 11.2 years.

During follow-up, 1,822 deaths occurred, and vitamin D deficiency at baseline was associated with a substantially increased hazard of all-cause mortality after adjustment for age, sex, body-mass index, smoking status, and physical activity (hazard ratio 1.62, 95% CI 1.41 to 1.87, p < 0.001).

The association was consistent across strata defined by age, sex, and season of blood draw, and was not materially attenuated by additional adjustment for pre-existing cardiovascular illness or diabetes.
These findings indicate that vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of all-cause mortality in adults in the general population.

title: Serum vitamin D deficiency and risk of death from any cause: findings from a Scandinavian population cohort.
abstract: Low vitamin D status is common in populations at higher latitudes and has been linked to a range of adverse health outcomes, but whether it independently predicts mortality remains debated.

We investigated the relationship between serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration and all-cause mortality in a prospective cohort of 7,210 adults recruited from the general population of a Scandinavian country and followed for a median of 14.6 years.
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured at baseline, and vitamin D deficiency was defined using the same threshold as prior population studies (below 30 nmol/L).

Participants with vitamin D deficiency at baseline had a higher rate of death from any cause during follow-up than participants with sufficient vitamin D status, corresponding to an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.55 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.81, p < 0.001) after adjustment for age, sex, smoking, body-mass index, and comorbidity burden.
The elevated mortality risk associated with vitamin D deficiency was present in both men and women and did not differ materially by age group.
This independent cohort confirms that vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of all-cause mortality in adults, consistent with findings from other populations.

title: Vitamin D deficiency is associated with increased mortality risk in a matched case-control study of hospitalized older adults.
abstract: Whether vitamin D status contributes to mortality risk independently of the acute illnesses that bring older adults to hospital has been unclear, and case-control designs offer a complementary approach to cohort studies for examining this question.

We conducted a matched case-control study comparing serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations, measured at admission, between 340 individuals aged 65 years or older who died within one year of hospital discharge and 340 surviving controls matched for age, sex, and primary admission diagnosis.
Vitamin D deficiency, defined as serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 nmol/L, at admission was more common among cases than controls (58% versus 34%).

In conditional logistic regression adjusting for comorbidity index, nutritional status, and length of stay, vitamin D deficiency was associated with substantially increased odds of death within one year (odds ratio 2.31, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.19, p < 0.001).
The association persisted after excluding individuals who died within 30 days of admission, arguing against reverse causation from terminal illness alone explaining the entire effect.
These findings support an association between vitamin D deficiency and increased mortality risk that is not fully accounted for by the severity of the presenting illness.

title: Nested case-control analysis links vitamin D deficiency to excess mortality in community-dwelling older adults.
abstract: Case-control designs nested within existing community cohorts allow efficient testing of biomarker associations with mortality without the cost of biobanking an entire cohort, and vitamin D status is a candidate marker for excess mortality risk in older populations.

From a community-based registry of adults aged 60 years and older, we identified 410 individuals who died during a ten-year surveillance period and matched each to two surviving controls of the same age, sex, and region of residence, then measured stored baseline serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations.
Cases had markedly lower baseline vitamin D concentrations than matched controls, and vitamin D deficiency at baseline was present in 52% of cases compared with 27% of controls.

After adjustment for baseline chronic illness burden, smoking, and body-mass index, vitamin D deficiency remained associated with increased mortality (odds ratio 2.04, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.79, p < 0.001).
The magnitude of the association was similar for cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular causes of death, suggesting a relationship that is not confined to a single underlying pathway.
This nested case-control analysis corroborates a link between vitamin D deficiency and excess mortality risk in older community-dwelling adults.

title: Is the association between vitamin D deficiency and mortality causal? A review of repletion trials and Mendelian randomization evidence.
abstract: Observational studies consistently report that adults with low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations have higher all-cause mortality than adults with sufficient vitamin D status, but whether this association reflects a causal effect of vitamin D itself remains contested.

Large randomized controlled trials of vitamin D repletion, including trials enrolling tens of thousands of participants and following them for five years or more, have generally failed to demonstrate a reduction in all-cause mortality among treated participants relative to placebo.

Mendelian randomization studies, which use genetic variants that raise or lower vitamin D concentration as instruments to probe causality, have likewise found little evidence that genetically predicted vitamin D level is associated with mortality risk.

These discrepancies have led some investigators to argue that low vitamin D status is a marker of poor underlying health, since reduced sun exposure, lower physical activity, obesity, and chronic inflammatory illness all lower circulating vitamin D, rather than a cause of death in its own right.

Others note that repletion trials typically enrol participants who are not severely deficient and may dose for too short a duration to reverse any causal pathway established over years of deficiency, so a null trial does not conclusively rule out a causal role for vitamin D status itself.

Reconciling the robust observational association with the largely null interventional and genetic evidence remains an open question in nutritional epidemiology, and the debate over confounding, reverse causation, and a genuine but hard-to-reverse causal pathway is unresolved.

title: Vitamin D signalling regulates calcium absorption and bone mineral density independently of mortality outcomes.
abstract: Vitamin D is a key regulator of intestinal calcium absorption and skeletal mineralization, and its receptor is expressed throughout osteoblasts and osteoclasts.

We reviewed the molecular pathways by which active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D promotes calcium transport across the intestinal epithelium and regulates osteoblast-mediated bone formation and osteoclast-mediated resorption.
Vitamin D receptor signalling upregulates transcription of calcium-binding proteins in enterocytes and modulates parathyroid hormone secretion, together maintaining serum calcium homeostasis.

In animal models, vitamin D receptor knockout produces rickets-like skeletal abnormalities and impaired mineralization that can be substantially corrected by a high-calcium diet independent of vitamin D status.
These findings describe the skeletal and calcium-homeostatic actions of vitamin D signalling and do not address any relationship between vitamin D status and mortality risk.
